doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Audience connection and memorable small-venue nights, including Romania
summary: Ries speaks about playing for the moment, small communities, and an acoustic night with Roma musicians in Romania.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah I commented to someone as we were going out the door I said, “I bet you didn’t expect the night was going to end like that.” It was terrific. Audience communication. And I think you — it’s obvious you learned from your father and maybe even from the Stones like about the entertainment factor involved in presenting music. I saw it.

Well I mean I try my best not to be like — you hate to say — well like you said you know one of the great ballads, “Willow Weep for Me” to the Stones’ that’s one of the most famous songs ever, “Satisfaction” has been covered by everyone from Aretha Franklin to Stevie Wonder to — well it’s just so famous, to the “Beer Barrel Polka” — everyone who knows a polka that’s probably the most well known polka. So it’s almost like I’m trying not to make it too kitsch or too like I’m not trying to go like you know ultra entertainment but it was like on that night, in that room with those people who were part of the mix, I mean how often are you going to have a polka accordion player sitting in the front with his accordion out and not make that part of the night? It’s like so — or a different night would be a different thing. You know like ‘cause I’m always if I have a friend that’s there I will always invite them onstage because then it brings a new element to the band you know. So I try to do what is happening right then, because that’s the most important thing, and I was mentioning this to Mr. Domenico today, we just had a cup of coffee before coming over here and there was talking about how nice it was to play in a small venue, even though there wasn’t that many people, some of the most beautiful evenings of sharing experiences are in small places. Because 50,000 people is amazing but then after the gig you’re not going to go across the street and have a bar — have a beer at with the people who just saw you and really develop like a community with the community of people who live there. But then also to include that, and one of the most incredible nights of my life was with this group of Roma musicians from Budapest, we

went to Romania to play a gig at this really cool venue, small place, and it was such a nice night we moved it out to the back deck because it was a full moon, perfect weather, about a hundred people sitting, it was ultra quiet it was like you could hear a pin drop. And people were so — it was a totally acoustic, no amplification, acoustic bass, acoustic piano, acoustic drums and it was like the connection with the audience with this beautiful night and all the people afterwards, we hung for hours talking to the local people. It was like those are the nights that are the most special because you’re not only connecting with the people on the stage who I have this great association with, but then oh my God you get to meet interesting people from Romania who love music and art and you talk about culture and literature, how about this book, and you’re like wow, then you really connect with this part of the world.
